title: Hard experiences
hook: a 2020 review estimated about 8 percent of meditators report unpleasant effects (Farias et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday: mindfulness in schools, and a trial that found the lessons no better than usual teaching. Your line was invite, don't force. Did you leave a door open for someone? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

Not every sit ends in peace. Someone closes their eyes for a few minutes of breathing, and instead of quiet, their heart starts racing. Or an old memory they'd packed away comes up with full force. Or the room starts to feel strangely unreal. The cheerful version of meditation skips this part. This path has been saying for days that it owes you the honest picture, and this is part of it: sometimes practice is hard, and not in a good way. Today is about what researchers found, what one old teacher wrote about his own breakdown, and how to know when to stop.
screen: `NOT EVERY SIT ENDS IN PEACE.` → `A RACING HEART, AN OLD MEMORY.` → `THE HONEST PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the numbers, carefully. A review led by Miguel Farias pooled studies that asked meditators about unpleasant effects. It estimated that about 8 percent reported at least one. Anxiety and low mood were among the most common. That's a minority. But it isn't zero, and it isn't nothing. Second, the old teachers knew. The Japanese Zen teacher Hakuin wrote about his own collapse in a text known as Idle Talk on a Night Boat. As he tells it, he pushed his practice so hard that his body and mind broke down, a condition he called Zen sickness. A hermit, he says, taught him a gentler practice that helped him recover. Zen has its own word for this. Third, the signs. Clinicians who study these experiences describe some warning signs worth knowing: panic that builds rather than passes, feeling detached or unreal, painful memories flooding in, sleep falling apart. Their practical advice is plain: open your eyes, feel your feet, move your body, shorten the sit or stop, and talk to someone. Fourth, what stopping means. Stopping isn't failing. Hakuin's own story turns on learning a gentler way. Knowing your edge is part of the practice, not a break from it.
screen: `ABOUT 8 PERCENT REPORTED ONE.` · `HAKUIN'S ZEN SICKNESS.` · `PANIC, UNREALITY, FLOODING.` · `STOPPING ISN'T FAILING.` · then, large: `KNOW WHEN TO STOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a sit with the exits marked. Keep your eyes open today, resting softly on the floor a little ahead of you. Feel both feet on the ground. Breathe normally. Now, gently, ask yourself what your own signs would be. A tight chest. A spinning head. Feeling far away. Name one or two, quietly. Then make the plan: if that comes, I open my eyes wide, look around the room, press my feet down, and stop. Rest in knowing the door is right there. The bell holds the time.
Hard experiences. A minority of meditators report unpleasant effects, and old teachers wrote about them too. Today's word.

Your line: know when to stop. Today, write your one or two signs somewhere private, with your plan beside them. Then you won't have to think when it matters. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Careful meditation teachers ask students to notice warning signs such as panic, feeling unreal or flooding memories, and to open their eyes, ground themselves, shorten or stop practice, and seek help when those signs appear.

original.note: Japanese, from Zen Buddhism: Zen sickness, the breakdown Hakuin describes from pushing practice too hard.
